content: Black hairy tongue is a condition in which the tongue develops an unusual dark and/or hairy appearance. In humans, this condition is benign and is caused by the overgrowth of a fungus on the top surface of the tongue. It is more frequently observed in elderly individuals and is associated with the use of antibiotics. Tobacco smokers are particularly prone to developing this condition. While the name suggests a black discoloration, the tongue can also appear brown, white, green, or pink, depending on secondary factors such as the use of certain mouthwashes or breath mints. The medical term for this condition is hairy tongue (lingua villosa), which occurs due to defective desquamation (shedding) of the filiform papillae on the tongue. This defective shedding can result from various factors, including poor oral hygiene, tooth loss (as a soft diet does not provide the mechanical scraping needed for normal desquamation), prolonged or excessive use of antibiotics, and radiation therapy to the head and neck. Individuals with hairy tongue are often coffee or tea drinkers and may use tobacco products. It is also more commonly observed in individuals who are HIV-positive or use intravenous drugs, although the condition itself does not have predictive value for these underlying issues. The shared lifestyle habits, such as poor oral hygiene, tobacco or marijuana use, and coffee consumption, are likely contributing factors. The hairy appearance typically affects the posterior (back) portion of the tongue and does not involve the underside of the tongue. Although the condition is not harmful and is usually asymptomatic, some patients may develop a secondary infection with Candida albicans (thrush). It is unclear whether hairy tongue predisposes individuals to thrush or if the underlying causes of hairy tongue also contribute to the development of thrush. Additionally, the use of medications like Pepto-Bismol can cause the tongue and stool to turn black. This discoloration is due to the chemical reaction between bismuth (a component of the medication) and sulfur in saliva, forming bismuth trisulfide. Treatment for hairy tongue primarily involves maintaining good oral hygiene. This includes regular brushing of the tongue with a toothbrush or using a tongue scraper to promote desquamation. If a candidal infection is suspected, antifungal medications may be necessary. In cases where the condition is linked to antibiotic use, it often resolves naturally once the antibiotic course is completed. In animals, a similar condition known as black tongue can occur in dogs. This is caused by a deficiency of niacin and is associated with ulcers and inflammation in the dog's oral cavity.
